chunks: The brother of Rumi ibn Umar bequeathed that all his wealth was for Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him). Amru said: Rumi informed me that he placed the will before Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said, this is what my brother has bequeathed to you. I began to read it to him, and he would say to me: Pause! and he would say: Take such and such, and I have gifted you such and such, until I reached the end of the will. I looked, and he had taken only the one-third. Amru said: So I said to him, you have ordered me to carry a third to you, and you have gifted me the two-thirds? He said: Yes. I said, shall I sell it and bring it to you? He said: No, fulfill it according to what is easy for you — do not sell anything.

key_terms.الثُّلُثَ: one-third (al-thuluth): the maximum share allowed for bequest under Islamic inheritance law
key_terms.الثُّلُثَيْنِ: two-thirds (al-thulthayn): the share gifted back by the Imam to the deceased's brother
key_terms.الْمَيْسُورِ: what is feasible/easy (al-maysur): the Imam's instruction to fulfill only what is within means, without hardship
key_terms.الْوَصِيَّةَ: will/bequest (wasiyya): a testamentary disposition of property, limited to one-third of the estate in Islamic law

ai.seo_question: What does this Al-Kafi hadith teach about the one-third rule in Islamic wills?
ai.summary: This hadith narrates a remarkable act of generosity by Imam Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): when presented with a will bequeathing him the entire estate of a deceased man, the Imam reviewed it item by item, directing what should be delivered to him and gifting the rest back to the deceased's brother, ultimately taking only the legal maximum of one-third. He further instructed the brother not to sell any assets to fulfill the bequest. In Shia Islamic jurisprudence, a person may bequest only up to one-third of their estate; the other two-thirds belong to the heirs. This hadith illustrates the Imam's profound generosity and practical concern for the deceased's family.
